title: Flour tortillas
subtitle: Soft flatbreads made with flour and fat, rested before cooking on a dry griddle
excerpt: Flour tortillas need fat and a rest. The lard or butter gets rubbed into the flour before the water goes in, giving the dough a short texture that rolls thin without snapping back. Resting after rolling is not optional; the gluten needs time to relax before the tortilla holds its shape on the pan.
sourceNotes: Flour tortillas are a staple of northern Mexican and Tex-Mex cooking, distinct from corn tortillas which use masa harina. The fat-rubbed, leavened dough method has been documented in Mexican cookery literature and is widely taught in culinary curricula covering flatbread technique.

recipe.freezeNotes: Stack cooked, cooled tortillas with baking paper between each and freeze in a bag for up to 3 months. Reheat from frozen directly in a dry pan for 30 seconds per side.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles cleanly. Weigh and pre-portion the dough balls before the resting period.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cooked tortillas keep in an airtight bag at room temperature for 2 days, or in the fridge for 1 week. Reheat in a dry pan.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Cooked in a dry cast-iron skillet or heavy frying pan over medium-high heat. No oil.

glossaryTerms.definition: The resting period between rolling and cooking a flour tortilla. Rolled dough springs back toward its original shape; rested dough stays flat because the gluten strands have had time to relax. Ten to fifteen minutes at room temperature is enough.

content.text: The key to a soft flour tortilla that rolls without tearing is

. Roll a ball of dough straight away and it springs back; rest it for 15 minutes and it stays wherever you put it. Baking powder gives a slight lift and keeps the finished tortilla soft rather than crackerlike.

items.prepNote: or unsalted butter, at room temperature

content.text: Combine flour, salt, and baking powder. Add the lard and rub it into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs with no visible lumps of fat.
Add the warm water a little at a time, mixing as you go. Work until a smooth, soft dough forms. Knead for 2 minutes; it should feel slightly tacky but not sticky.
Divide into 8 equal balls (about 77 g each). Cover and rest for 30 minutes.
On a lightly floured surface, roll one ball into a thin circle of about 25 cm. It does not need to be a perfect circle. Cover and rest for at least 10 minutes before cooking.
Heat a cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat until a drop of water evaporates on contact. Add the tortilla; no oil.

Cook for about 45 to 60 seconds until light brown spots appear on the underside. Flip and cook for a further 30 to 45 seconds. The tortilla should puff in places. Stack cooked tortillas under a clean cloth to keep them soft.

Lard produces a softer, more pliable tortilla than butter because it contains no water and has a different fat structure. Butter works well and is fine for most purposes. Avoid oil: it makes the tortilla oily rather than short.
